Closures

A function that remembers variables from where it was created, not from where it's called.

This is plain JavaScript, not Express — but it's worth stopping on deliberately, because the very next topic's code doesn't make sense without it, and it's not something Laravel/PHP work tends to build up a feel for.

A closure is a function that "remembers" the variables that were in scope where it was defined, even after that outer code has finished running:

function makeGreeter(name) {
  // `name` is a normal local variable of makeGreeter — nothing special yet.
  return function () {
    // This inner function "closes over" `name`. It keeps access to it even
    // after makeGreeter has already returned.
    console.log(`Hello, ${name}!`);
  };
}

const greetJane = makeGreeter('Jane');
const greetAmir = makeGreeter('Amir');

greetJane(); // "Hello, Jane!"
greetAmir(); // "Hello, Amir!"

makeGreeter runs, returns its inner function, and finishes — but greetJane and greetAmir each still have their own remembered name, because each call to makeGreeter created a fresh one. That's the part with no real PHP equivalent: a PHP function's local variables are simply gone once it returns.

Why this matters here: a function that returns another function like this is often called a factory — and the very next topic's asyncHandler is exactly that shape: a function that takes something in and returns a new function which remembers it. Once this pattern is familiar in isolation, that code reads as "oh, it's just a closure" instead of a wall of unfamiliar syntax.
